concepts.title: Stereo Anaglyph
concepts.one_liner: A stereo anaglyph uses color filters to deliver separate images to each eye, creating a 3D effect from two laterally displaced camera views.
concepts.content: A stereo anaglyph is a 3D image created using two cameras displaced laterally from one another. In this format, the right camera's image appears in red and the left camera's image appears in cyan. When viewed with a red filter over the left eye and a cyan filter over the right, each eye sees only its corresponding camera's image, allowing the scene to pop out into a three-dimensional stereo image. The relative displacement between the images of objects changes as a function of their depth, which enables the 3D interpretation.
concepts.motivation_md: Anaglyphs provide a simple way to display 3D depth information on standard 2D screens or print media using inexpensive colored glasses.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses red and cyan filters to separate left and right eye views.

motivation.text: Note that the relative displacement between each camera's image of the smokestacks changes as a function of their depth, which allows us to form a 3D interpretation of the ship when viewing the image with the glasses.

concepts.title: Image Rectification
concepts.one_liner: Image rectification is a manipulation used to align the locus of potential matches along a pixel row.
concepts.content: Image rectification is a manipulation often used to place the locus of potential matches along a pixel row.
concepts.motivation_md: By aligning corresponding features along horizontal rows, rectification simplifies the search for matching points in stereo pairs from a 2D search to a 1D search.

concepts.title: Triangulation for Distance Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Triangulation estimates the distance to an object by measuring angles from two observation points separated by a known distance.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Two methods to estimate the distance of a boat from the coast. (left) The first method uses a single observation point, with knowledge of the observer's height above the water. (right) The second...)

Triangulation is a method to estimate the distance $d$ of an object from a baseline. It requires two different observation points separated by a distance $t$. At each point, the angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ between the direction of the object and the line connecting the two observation points are measured. The distance is then calculated using the relation: $$d = t \frac{\sin (\alpha) \sin (\beta)}{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}$$ For this method to be effective, the distance $t$ must be large enough so that the angles are significantly different from $90$ degrees.
concepts.motivation_md: Triangulation allows for the calculation of distances to remote objects that cannot be measured directly, provided two vantage points and the angles to the target are known.
concepts.recap_md: - Requires two observation points and a known baseline distance $t$.

key_passage.text: The second method requires two different observation points along the coast separated by a distance t. At each point, we measure the angles, α and β, between the direction of the boat and the line connecting the two observation points. Then we can apply the following relation: d = t sin(α) sin(β)/sin(α+β) This method is called triangulation.

motivation.text: For it to work we need a large distance t so that the angles are significantly different from 90 degrees.

concepts.title: Parallax Effect
concepts.one_liner: The parallax effect is the relative displacement of features across two images, which relates to the distance between the observer and the scene.
concepts.content: The parallax effect is the relative displacement of features across two images. This displacement is related to the distance between the observer and the observed scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Parallax is the fundamental geometric principle that allows biological and computer vision systems to perceive depth from multiple viewpoints.

concepts.title: Harris Corner Detector
concepts.one_liner: The Harris corner detector identifies image points that are easy to localize by evaluating how the sum of squared intensity differences over an image patch changes under small translations.
concepts.content:
Good image features are positions in the image that are easy to localize given only the image intensities. The Harris corner detector identifies these points by evaluating how the sum of squared intensity differences over an image patch change under a small translation of the image. If the squared intensity changes quickly with patch translation in every direction, then the region contains a good image feature.

To derive the detector, we treat an image as a continuous function $\ell(x,y)$. For a small translation $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$, the squared intensity difference $E(\Delta x, \Delta y)$ summed over a small image patch $P$ is:
$$E(\Delta x, \Delta y) = \sum_{(x, y) \in P} \left( \ell(x,y) - \ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) \right)^2$$

Expanding $\ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y)$ using a Taylor series about $\ell(x, y)$ yields:
$$\ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) \approx \ell(x, y) + \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \Delta x + \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \Delta y$$

Substituting this into the energy equation and writing it in matrix form gives:
$$E(\Delta x, \Delta y) \approx \left[ \Delta x ~~ \Delta y \right] \mathbf{M} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Delta x \\ \Delta y \end{array} \right]$$
where
$$\mathbf{M} = \sum_{(n, m) \in P} \begin{bmatrix} (\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x})^2 & \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \\ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} & (\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y})^2 \end{bmatrix}$$

The smallest eigenvalue, $\lambda_{\mbox{min}}$, of the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ indicates the smallest possible change of image intensities under translation in any direction. To detect corners, one identifies points where $\lambda_{\mbox{min}} > \lambda_c$ for a chosen threshold $\lambda_c$.

[FIGURE:c647fcb81431db39]

[FIGURE:c1856c0bb1300e0f]

concepts.title: SIFT Image Descriptors
concepts.one_liner: SIFT uses histograms of oriented filter responses to create image descriptors that are sensitive to local structure but robust to lighting and location changes.
concepts.content:
Matching corresponding image features requires a local description of the image region to allow matching like regions across two images. SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) uses histograms of oriented filter responses to create an image descriptor that is sensitive to local image structure, but insensitive to minor changes in lighting or location which may occur across the two images of a stereo pair.

Local orientation is a powerful representation because images of the same object under different lighting conditions can look quite different in pixel intensities but very similar in their local orientation. SIFT descriptors exploit this by taking histograms of local orientation over local spatial regions, which further allows the descriptors to be robust to small image translations.

[FIGURE:faa7107c0d4f9db0]

[FIGURE:d0b75366352a79a7]
concepts.motivation_md: Raw pixel values are highly sensitive to lighting and viewpoint changes. SIFT provides a robust way to describe local image patches so they can be accurately matched even when the environment or camera position changes.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses histograms of oriented gradients to describe local image patches.

concepts.title: Interpolation between feature matches
concepts.one_liner: Depth between matched feature points can be interpolated using probabilistic methods or dynamic programming to approximate a global solution for stereo shape inference.
concepts.content:
Methods to interpolate depth between the depths of matched points include probabilistic methods such as belief propagation. Under assumptions about the local spatial relationships between depth values, optimal shapes can be inferred provided the spatial structure over which inference is performed is a chain or a tree. 

Another approach uses dynamic programming, which has the same constraints on spatial structure for exact inference. An example is semiglobal matching (SGM), which applies one-dimensional processing over many different orientations to approximate a global solution to the stereo shape inference problem.
concepts.motivation_md: Feature matching only provides depth at specific points. To create a dense depth map, we need techniques to intelligently fill in the gaps between these points based on spatial consistency.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses belief propagation or dynamic programming to infer depth between sparse matches.

concepts.title: Epipolar plane
concepts.one_liner: The epipolar plane is the plane containing the two camera origins and a specific 3D point in the world.
concepts.content:
The epipolar plane is defined within the geometry of a stereo pair. Given a 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, in the world, the epipolar plane is the plane that contains the two camera origins and that 3D point.

concepts.title: Epipoles
concepts.one_liner: Epipoles are the points where the line connecting camera origins intersects the camera planes.
concepts.content:
The epipoles are the intersection points between the line that connects both camera origins and the camera planes. Unlike the epipolar plane and lines, the epipoles' location does not depend on the point $\mathbf{P}$. Consequently, all epipolar lines for any point in the scene intersect at these same epipoles.

concepts.title: Essential matrix
concepts.one_liner: The essential matrix relates the 3D coordinates of a point viewed by two cameras, capturing the relative rotation and translation between them.
concepts.content:
The essential matrix $\mathbf{E}$ relates the coordinates of a 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ as seen by two cameras. If $\mathbf{P}_1$ and $\mathbf{P}_2$ are the coordinates in the first and second camera systems respectively, they are related by $\mathbf{P}_2 = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_1 + \mathbf{T}$. 

By taking the cross product with $\mathbf{T}$ and the dot product with $\mathbf{P}_2$, we derive the relationship:
$$\mathbf{P}_2^\mathsf{T}\left( \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{R} \right) \mathbf{P}_1 = 0$$

The essential matrix is defined as $\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{T}_{\times} \mathbf{R}$, where $\mathbf{T}_{\times}$ is the skew-symmetric matrix representing the cross product with $\mathbf{T}$. This leads to the epipolar constraint for image coordinates $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ (assuming focal length $f=1$):
$$\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$$

Properties of the essential matrix:
- It has five degrees of freedom (three for rotation, three for translation, minus one for global scaling).
- It has rank 2.
- It has two identical non-zero singular values and one zero singular value.
concepts.motivation_md: The essential matrix provides a mathematical way to enforce the geometric constraints of a stereo system using only the relative pose of the cameras, allowing us to relate points in one view to lines in another.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates calibrated camera coordinates via the constraint $\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$.

key_passage.text: The matrix $\mathbf{E}$ is called the **essential matrix** and it corresponds to: $$\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{T}_{\times} \mathbf{R}$$ This results in the relationship: $$\mathbf{P}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{P}_1 = 0$$

motivation.text: This equation relates the coordinates of the two projections of a 3D point into two cameras. If we fix the coordinates from one of the cameras, the equation reduces to the equation of a line for the coordinates of the other camera, which is consistent with the geometric reasoning that we made before.

concepts.title: Fundamental matrix
concepts.one_liner: The fundamental matrix relates pixel coordinates between two images in a stereo pair, incorporating both extrinsic and intrinsic camera parameters.
concepts.content:
The fundamental matrix $\mathbf{F}$ relates image coordinates in pixels (homogeneous coordinates $\mathbf{c}=[n,m,1]^\mathsf{T}$) between two cameras. It incorporates intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$ (such as pixel size and origin) into the epipolar constraint. The relationship is expressed as:
$$\mathbf{c}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{F} \mathbf{c}_1 = 0$$

The fundamental matrix is related to the essential matrix $\mathbf{E}$ via the intrinsic matrix:
$$\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{K}^{\mathsf{T}}$$

Like the essential matrix, the fundamental matrix has rank 2. It has 7 degrees of freedom: out of 9 total elements, one is lost to scale ambiguity and one is lost because the determinant must be zero.
concepts.motivation_md: While the essential matrix works with calibrated camera coordinates, the fundamental matrix allows us to relate raw pixel coordinates directly, which is essential when the internal camera parameters are known but not yet removed from the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates raw pixel coordinates across two views using $\mathbf{c}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{F} \mathbf{c}_1 = 0$.

concepts.title: Disparity vs Depth Representation
concepts.one_liner: Estimating 3D structure can be done via disparity or depth, with disparity often being easier to model due to its independence from camera parameters and uniform noise characteristics.
concepts.content: When estimating the 3D structure of a scene, we can represent the output as either disparity or depth. Disparity is often easier to estimate because it is independent of camera parameters. Furthermore, modeling noise is more straightforward with disparity, as we can assume noise is independent of the disparity value itself. In contrast, when using depth, the estimation error tends to increase for more distant points.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing between disparity and depth is a fundamental design decision in stereo vision. Disparity is preferred for its mathematical simplicity and stable noise properties, whereas depth is the ultimate physical quantity of interest but suffers from increasing error at a distance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Disparity is independent of camera parameters and has noise characteristics that are easier to model.
 - Depth estimation error increases for points that are further away from the camera.

concepts.title: Disparity Regularization for Planar Surfaces
concepts.one_liner: For flat surfaces, the second-order derivative of disparity along any spatial direction is zero, a property that does not hold for depth.
concepts.content: An interesting property of disparity is that for flat surfaces, the second-order derivative along any spatial direction, $\mathbf{x}$, is zero: $$\frac{\partial^2 d}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2}  = 0.$$ This equality does not hold for depth. This property allows for the introduction of a simple regularization term that favors planarity in the estimated scene.
concepts.motivation_md: This mathematical property provides a simple way to enforce a 'smoothness' or 'planarity' constraint in computer vision algorithms, helping to resolve ambiguities in disparity estimation for flat objects.

concepts.title: Converting Disparity to Depth
concepts.one_liner: Depth is calculated by taking the inverse of the disparity value for a given pixel.
concepts.content: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d\left[n,m \right]$ into depth values $z\left[n,m \right]$, we need to invert the disparity: $$\begin{aligned} z \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{ d \left[n,m \right] } \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: While algorithms often compute disparity for numerical stability, humans and robots require depth (actual distance) to navigate or interact with the 3D world.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth $z$ is the reciprocal of disparity $d$.
 - The conversion is performed per-pixel using the formula $z = 1/d$.

concepts.title: Recovering World Coordinates from Depth
concepts.one_liner: World coordinates in the camera frame are recovered by multiplying the pixel's depth by the inverse of the intrinsic camera matrix.
concepts.content: To recover the world coordinates for every pixel, we assume a pinhole camera model. Using the depth $z \left[n,m \right]$ and the intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$, we obtain the 3D coordinates for a pixel with image coordinates $[n,m]$ in the camera reference frame as: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = z\left[n,m \right] \times \mathbf{K}^{-1} \times \begin{bmatrix} n \\ m \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ Note that $\mathbf{K}$ represents the intrinsic camera parameters for the reference image.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the 3D location of objects relative to the camera is essential for tasks like mapping, obstacle avoidance, and 3D modeling.
concepts.recap_md:
- 3D coordinates are recovered using depth and the inverse intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}^{-1}$.
 - The calculation transforms 2D image coordinates $[n, m]$ into 3D camera-frame coordinates $[X, Y, Z]$.

concepts.title: Two-Stage Neural Networks for Stereo
concepts.one_liner: Two-stage stereo networks use shared-weight feature extraction followed by a 3D convolutional neural net to aggregate matching costs and estimate disparity.
concepts.content:
Given two images, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$, the disparity at each location can be computed by a function $\hat{\mathbf{d}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$. The objective is to minimize the difference between estimated disparities $\hat{\mathbf{d}}$ and ground truth $\mathbf{d}$, often using a loss function such as $J(\theta) = \sum_t \left| \mathbf{d} - f_{\theta} (\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) \right|^2$. 

When matching and filtering are implemented separately, a common formulation uses one neural network $g$ to extract features from both images and another network $c$ to compute matching costs: $f(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) = c \left( g(\mathbf{v}_1), g(\mathbf{v}_2) \right)$. A typical approach involves:
- Rectifying the stereo pair so scanlines align.
- Extracting features using a pair of networks with shared weights.
- Forming a 3D cost volume representing visual evidence of matches for each pixel and possible disparity.
- Applying a 3D convolutional neural net (CNN) to aggregate costs over the volume to estimate the best disparity for each pixel. This replaces traditional regularization steps like SGM with improved performance.

(see figure: Block diagram of CNN stereo processing, abstracted from the block diagrams of @Chang2018, @Zhang2019GANet, @Kendall2017)
concepts.motivation_md: Modern deep learning approaches improve upon traditional stereo matching by learning complex feature representations and cost aggregation strategies directly from data, leading to higher accuracy in challenging scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Stereo pairs are rectified and processed through shared-weight networks for feature extraction.
 - A 3D cost volume is formed and processed by a 3D CNN to estimate the final disparity map.
 - This neural approach effectively performs the role of regularization in traditional stereo algorithms.

concepts.title: Random Dot Stereograms
concepts.one_liner: Random dot stereograms demonstrate that humans can perceive depth using the relative displacement of features even in the absence of other depth cues.
concepts.content:
Random dot stereograms, introduced by Bela Julesz, are a beautiful demonstration that humans can perceive depth using the relative displacement of features across two views even in the absence of any other depth cues. The random images contain no recognizable features and are quite different from the statistics of the natural world. But this seems not to affect our ability to compute the displacements between the two images and perceive 3D structure.

concepts.title: Anaglyph Pinhole Camera
concepts.one_liner: An anaglyph pinhole camera captures stereo images in a single shot by using two pinholes with different color filters.
concepts.content:
A stereo pinhole camera can be built to produce anaglyph images, like the one in @fig-titanic, in a single shot by making two pinholes instead of just one. By placing different color filters on each hole, the camera produces an image that is the superposition of two images taken from slightly different viewpoints, each with a different color. To see the 3D image, the picture is viewed by placing the same color filters in front of the eyes, such as red and blue glasses.

(see figure: One way of playing with pinhole cameras is to build an anaglyph pinhole camera. The anaglyph pinhole camera captures stereo images by projecting an anaglyph image on the projection plane.)

Experimental results show that the distance between pinholes affects 3D perception; for example, a 1.5 in distance may be easier to fuse than 3 in. Because filters reduce the light entering the camera, longer exposure times are required to maintain image quality. While increasing the distance between pinholes increases the parallax effect and the range of 3D information, if the images are too far apart, the visual system will not be able to fuse them.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique provides a simple way to capture 3D depth information in a single exposure by encoding two different perspectives into distinct color channels.

Then, to see the 3D image we can look at the picture by placing the same color filters in front of our eyes.

concepts.title: Stereo Triangulation
concepts.one_liner: Stereo triangulation estimates the depth of points in the world by comparing images from two spatially offset cameras.
concepts.content:
The task of stereo is to triangulate the depth of points in the world by comparing the images from two spatially offset cameras. To triangulate depth, we must describe how image positions in the stereo pair relate to depth in the 3D world. In a simple setting where two identical, calibrated cameras are translated horizontally with parallel optical axes, a 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ projects to $[x_L,y_L]^\mathsf{T}$ in the left camera and $[x_R,y_R]^\mathsf{T}$ in the right camera. Because of the horizontal alignment, $y_L=y_R$. Using similar triangles, the depth $Z$ can be calculated as:

$$Z =  \frac{fT}{x_L-x_R}$$

where $f$ is the focal length and $T$ is the horizontal offset (baseline) between the cameras. The difference in horizontal position $x_L - x_R$ is called the disparity, which is inversely proportional to the depth $Z$.
concepts.motivation_md: Triangulation provides the mathematical basis for recovering 3D scene structure from 2D images by exploiting the geometric relationship between multiple viewpoints.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth is calculated using similar triangles based on camera focal length and the baseline distance between cameras.

concepts.title: Disparity
concepts.one_liner: Disparity is the difference in horizontal position of a world point as seen in the left and right camera images.
concepts.content: The difference in horizontal position of any given world point, $\mathbf{P}$, as seen in the left and right camera images, $x_L - x_R$, is called the disparity. For a configuration of two cameras with parallel orientation, disparity is inversely proportional to the depth $Z$ of the point $\mathbf{P}$. The task of inferring depth in a stereo pair reduces to measuring this disparity everywhere.

concepts.title: The Stereo Matching Problem
concepts.one_liner: Stereo matching is the problem of identifying which points in one image correspond to the same 3D point in another image.
concepts.content:
The stereo matching problem involves determining which points in one camera's image correspond to the same 3D point in another camera's image. This is the crux of the stereo problem, as images are complex and correspondences are not immediately known. 

[FIGURE:5b3ceb105441e961]

[FIGURE:8bc44da026c71495]

A naive algorithm searching for pixels of the same intensity often fails due to factors like lack of texture, image noise, specularities, and occlusions. Effective approaches often involve finding features and matching them across images, then interpolating or filtering these matches to obtain a reliable disparity estimate everywhere. These two steps are often referred to as matching and filtering.
concepts.motivation_md: Solving the matching problem is a prerequisite for calculating disparity; without accurate correspondences, depth cannot be triangulated in complex scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Stereo matching identifies corresponding features between two views to calculate disparity.

key_passage.text: The task of finding disparity at each point is often broken into two parts: (1) finding features, and matching the features across images, and (2) interpolating between, or adjusting, the feature matches to obtain a reliable disparity estimate everywhere.

motivation.text: But in reality the two images will be complex and we will not know which points in one camera correspond to the same 3D point on the other camera. This requires solving the stereo matching problem.

concepts.title: Disparity Space Image
concepts.one_liner: A disparity space image represents matching errors for a range of disparity offsets across horizontal positions.
concepts.content: The disparity space image is a configuration where matching errors, such as the squared difference of intensity differences from offset versions of the same row in a stereo pair, are plotted for a range of disparity offsets. These offsets are typically plotted vertically as a function of horizontal position. This representation helps identify the best matches, though raw intensity matches can be noisy and may require edge-preserving filters to produce reliable results.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a structured way to evaluate matching costs across all possible disparities, facilitating the use of optimization techniques to find the most likely depth estimates.

The planarity property is defined specifically as a second-order derivative of the disparity map.
Converting to depth requires the disparity value as the input to the inverse operation.
In stereo pipelines, depth is typically calculated from disparity before being used to recover world coordinates.
The primary objective of these neural networks is to estimate a disparity map from a stereo pair.
Stereo networks typically require rectified images so that matching can be performed along horizontal scanlines.
Free fusion is a technique to perceive 3D structure by manually aligning the parallax-displaced images from each eye.
Random dot stereograms isolate the parallax effect as the sole source of depth information, proving its sufficiency for 3D perception.

The fundamental matrix is a generalization of the essential matrix that maps pixel coordinates by including intrinsic parameters.
